stem: What is the primary role of ServiceNow Discovery in populating the CMDB?

options.text: To automatically find devices and applications on the network and create/update their CIs
To approve change requests for new hardware
To calculate CMDB Health scores
To define the CSDM service model

rationale: Discovery is an ingestion engine: it probes the network, identifies devices, servers, and the software running on them, and creates or updates the corresponding CIs (through IRE). It's one of the main automated ways the CMDB stays populated and current.

distractor_notes.B: Change approval is a Change Management process, not Discovery.
distractor_notes.C: Health scoring is the Insight layer, not Discovery's job.
distractor_notes.D: CSDM is a modeling framework; Discovery feeds data into it but doesn't define it.

stem: What is the function of a MID Server in Discovery and integrations?

options.text: It is a lightweight application that runs inside the customer network to securely execute probes/commands and relay data to the ServiceNow instance
It is a cloud-only service that never touches the customer network
It is a CMDB table
It is a type of CI relationship

rationale: The MID (Management, Instrumentation, and Discovery) Server sits inside the customer's network. It executes probes and patterns against local devices and passes results back to the instance — bridging the cloud instance and on-prem infrastructure without exposing internal systems directly.

distractor_notes.B: The MID Server's whole point is to operate within the customer network.
distractor_notes.C: It's a runtime component, not a database table.
distractor_notes.D: It isn't a relationship type; it's an execution agent.

stem: What is a Service Graph Connector?

options.text: A productized, IRE-based integration that imports third-party data into the CMDB following CSDM and identification rules
A physical cable connecting two servers
A dashboard widget
A type of incident

rationale: Service Graph Connectors are pre-built integrations that bring external data sources into the CMDB the right way — through IRE, mapped to the correct classes, aligned to CSDM. They standardize third-party ingestion so it respects identification and reconciliation rather than dumping raw data.

distractor_notes.B: It's a software integration, not a physical cable.
distractor_notes.C: It's an ingestion integration, not a dashboard component.
distractor_notes.D: It has nothing to do with incidents.

stem: When Discovery or a Service Graph Connector brings data in, why should it pass through IRE rather than writing directly to CI tables?

options.text: So identification prevents duplicates and reconciliation protects authoritative attributes
So the data loads more slowly
So the MID Server can be turned off
So Discovery patterns are deleted

rationale: IRE is the single front door regardless of source. Routing ingestion through it means every incoming record is matched (no duplicates) and reconciled (no unauthorized overwrites). Bypassing IRE on ingestion is the fastest route to a polluted CMDB.

distractor_notes.B: The benefit is data integrity, not slower loading.
distractor_notes.C: IRE and the MID Server serve different roles; IRE doesn't replace the MID Server.
distractor_notes.D: IRE processing doesn't delete patterns.

stem: What is IntegrationHub ETL used for in the context of CMDB ingestion?

options.text: A guided tool to transform and map third-party import data to CMDB classes/attributes and load it via IRE
A tool for editing email templates
A network packet sniffer
A change calendar

rationale: IntegrationHub ETL provides a guided, low-code way to map and transform incoming third-party data onto the right CMDB classes and attributes, then load it through IRE. It's how custom data sources are onboarded cleanly when no packaged connector exists.

distractor_notes.B: It's a data transformation/mapping tool, not an email editor.
distractor_notes.C: It transforms import data; it isn't a packet capture tool.
distractor_notes.D: It has nothing to do with change calendars.

stem: Horizontal Discovery and Top-down (Service) Mapping differ in what fundamental way?

options.text: Horizontal Discovery finds infrastructure CIs broadly
They are the same feature
Horizontal Discovery only works on printers
Service Mapping deletes CIs

rationale: Horizontal Discovery scans broadly to populate infrastructure CIs and their direct relationships. Service Mapping works top-down from a defined entry point (like a URL) to trace the specific CIs and dependencies that make up a business service — a targeted, service-centric view rather than a broad sweep.

distractor_notes.B: They're complementary but distinct approaches.
distractor_notes.C: Horizontal Discovery covers a wide range of infrastructure, not just printers.
distractor_notes.D: Service Mapping builds maps; it doesn't delete CIs.

stem: What is the role of an import set table and transform map in data ingestion?

options.text: The import set stages incoming source rows
They approve changes automatically
They are used only for sending emails
They store user passwords

rationale: Imports use a two-step staging pattern: raw source rows land in an import set table, then a transform map defines how each field maps to the target CMDB table and applies any coalescing/transform logic. For CMDB targets this should route through IRE so identification and reconciliation apply.

distractor_notes.B: Imports load data; they don't approve changes.
distractor_notes.C: Import sets stage data for loading, not email sending.
distractor_notes.D: They don't store passwords.

stem: An organization wants to import data from a well-known third-party tool into the CMDB with minimal custom development and full CSDM alignment. What should they look for first?

options.text: A certified Service Graph Connector for that tool on the ServiceNow Store
A way to write directly to cmdb_ci with a script
A new incident category
A UI policy

rationale: For popular sources, a certified Service Graph Connector is the preferred path: it's pre-built, IRE-based, and CSDM-aligned, minimizing custom work and ensuring clean ingestion. You only fall back to ETL or custom integration when no suitable connector exists.

distractor_notes.B: Direct scripted writes bypass IRE and CSDM alignment — the opposite of the goal.
distractor_notes.C: Incident categories are unrelated to CMDB ingestion.
distractor_notes.D: A UI policy controls form behavior, not data import.

stem: In modern Discovery, what is a 'pattern'?

options.text: A set of declarative operations that defines how to probe a target and extract CI data, used instead of legacy probe/sensor scripting
A scheduled email
A CMDB Health threshold
A type of business service

rationale: Discovery patterns are declarative definitions — built in Pattern Designer — that specify how to interrogate a target and parse out CI attributes and relationships. They're the maintainable, low-code successor to the older probe-and-sensor scripting approach.

distractor_notes.B: Patterns drive discovery logic, not email scheduling.
distractor_notes.C: Health thresholds are an Insight concept, not a Discovery pattern.
distractor_notes.D: A pattern is discovery logic, not a service object.

stem: A Discovery schedule fails for an entire subnet with credential errors. Which area is the most likely first thing to check?

options.text: The credentials configured for the MID Server to access those targets
The CMDB Health dashboard colors
The CSDM domain definitions
The incident SLA policy

rationale: Credential errors across a subnet point straight at access: the credentials the MID Server uses to authenticate to those devices are missing, wrong, or lack permission. Verifying and fixing the credential configuration is the logical first diagnostic step.

distractor_notes.B: Dashboard colors have nothing to do with discovery credentials.
distractor_notes.C: CSDM domain definitions don't cause credential authentication failures.
distractor_notes.D: Incident SLAs are unrelated to Discovery access.

stem: A custom integration loads servers via an import set but creates duplicates each run. Inspection shows the transform writes straight to cmdb_ci_server. What is the recommended correction?

options.text: Route the load through the Identification and Reconciliation engine
Run the import twice as fast
Disable the CMDB Health dashboard
Add more columns to the import set table

rationale: Writing directly to the CI table skips identification, so every run inserts anew — hence the duplicates. The fix is to send the load through IRE (via an IRE-aware transform or the CMDB API) so incoming rows are matched to existing CIs instead of blindly inserted.

distractor_notes.B: Speed doesn't address the missing identification step.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling the dashboard hides the symptom, not the cause.
distractor_notes.D: Extra columns don't make the load match existing CIs.

stem: Which TWO advantages do certified Service Graph Connectors provide over building a custom integration from scratch?

options.text: They are pre-mapped to CMDB classes and use IRE for clean identification
They are tested/certified for CSDM alignment
They eliminate the need for any data source
They automatically write the company's financial reports

rationale: Packaged connectors save effort and risk: the class mapping and IRE integration are already built, and the connector is certified to align with CSDM. You still need the underlying source, and they certainly don't produce financial reports — but they get third-party data in correctly with far less custom work.

distractor_notes.C: Connectors ingest from a source; they don't remove the need for one.
distractor_notes.D: Financial reporting is entirely unrelated to CMDB connectors.

stem: A Configuration Manager has configured multiple data sources that are all authorized to update the same class and the same set of class attributes in the CMDB. What can the Configuration Manager do to control which data source's value should be kept?

options.text: Assign a priority to each data source in the reconciliation rules
Manually run the data source updates in the correct order each time
Configure data refresh rules with a specific time period
Assign a run order to each data source in the identification rules

rationale: When several authorized sources write the same attributes, reconciliation rules with data-source priority decide the winner. The higher-priority source's value is retained, giving deterministic control instead of last-write-wins — exactly the multisource problem reconciliation is built to solve.

distractor_notes.B: Manual ordering doesn't scale and isn't how the platform arbitrates attribute authority.
distractor_notes.C: Refresh timing controls when sources run, not which value wins on conflict.
distractor_notes.D: Identification rules resolve identity (which CI), not which source is authoritative for an attribute — that's reconciliation.

references.title: Reconciliation rules and data source priority

stem: An Apache Web Server identification rule uses criterion attributes Class, Configuration file, and Version. An Apache Web Server CI discovered yesterday is discovered again today with the same identifying values. What happens?

options.text: The existing Apache Web Server CI is reconciled and its attributes
A duplicate CI error stops all discovery
The CI is reclassified to a generic Web Server CI
A new, separate Apache Web Server CI is created

rationale: Because the criterion attributes match an existing CI, IRE identifies it as the same record and updates it rather than inserting a new one. That match-and-update behavior is precisely how identification rules prevent duplicates across repeated discoveries.

distractor_notes.B: A successful match isn't an error; IRE updates the matched CI.
distractor_notes.C: Matching identity doesn't trigger reclassification of the class.
distractor_notes.D: Creating a new CI is what happens when nothing matches — here the criteria match.

stem: A CMDB Administrator imported data from a third-party source using a Service Graph Connector and wants to review the specific field-to-field mappings used for the import. Which feature shows that information?

options.text: IntegrationHub ETL
Integration Hub (spokes/flows)
CMDB Integrations Dashboard
The incident form

rationale: Service Graph Connectors are built on IntegrationHub ETL, and the ETL interface is where the field-to-field mappings (source attribute to CMDB class/attribute) are defined and reviewed. That's the guided view an admin opens to inspect how imported data was mapped.

distractor_notes.B: IntegrationHub provides spokes/flows for actions; the ETL mapping view is the specific tool for CMDB field mappings.
distractor_notes.C: There isn't a generic 'CMDB Integrations Dashboard' that exposes the ETL field mappings; ETL itself does.
distractor_notes.D: The incident form is unrelated to import mappings.

stem: A CMDB Administrator needs the fastest time-to-value solution to ingest, manage, and maintain Windows computer CIs and relationships from Microsoft SCCM. Which approach accomplishes this?

options.text: The SCCM Service Graph Connector
An import set with a JDBC data source and custom transform maps
IntegrationHub ETL built from scratch with the Robust Transform Engine
The SCCM Usage Metering spoke

rationale: For a well-known source like SCCM, the certified Service Graph Connector is the fastest path to value: the class mappings, IRE integration, and CSDM alignment are pre-built. Custom import sets or ground-up ETL work all require significant configuration the connector already provides.

distractor_notes.B: A JDBC import with custom transforms is more build-and-maintain effort than a packaged connector.
distractor_notes.C: Building ETL from scratch is flexible but slower to value than the ready-made connector.
distractor_notes.D: Usage metering is a different function, not a CMDB ingestion connector for computer CIs.

stem: A CMDB Administrator changes the query for the SCCM Service Graph Connector (a customization). What is an impact of this change?

options.text: Updates for the SCCM Service Graph Connector will be skipped during upgrades because the mapping was customized
The connector's scheduled jobs are deleted automatically
The data source for the connector is marked Inactive
The customization is fully supported and auto-merged on upgrade

rationale: Customizing a connector's out-of-box mappings/queries means those records are no longer the shipped version, so connector updates that touch them are skipped on upgrade to avoid overwriting your changes. Customizations also fall outside ServiceNow support, which is the trade-off for modifying a packaged connector.

distractor_notes.B: Changing the query doesn't delete scheduled jobs.
distractor_notes.C: The data source isn't auto-deactivated by editing a query.
distractor_notes.D: Customizations are not auto-merged and are customer-supported, not vendor-supported.

stem: A CMDB Administrator must prevent duplicate CI creation when import sets load CI data from vendor shipment files. What is the recommended way to do this?

options.text: Call the CMDBTransformUtil API in the transform script so the load runs through IRE identification
Set coalesce on two fields in the transform map and write directly to the CI table
Manually delete duplicates after each import
Disable the transform map

rationale: To get identification (and thus duplicate prevention) from a transform map, route the load through IRE using the CMDBTransformUtil script API. That applies the class's identifier entries during the import so incoming rows match existing CIs instead of inserting new ones.

distractor_notes.B: Coalescing on a couple of fields and writing straight to the CI table bypasses IRE's full identification and still risks duplicates.
distractor_notes.C: Cleaning up after the fact treats the symptom, not the cause.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling the transform map stops the import entirely rather than fixing duplication.

stem: Which TWO categories of Service Graph Connectors are available to integrate third-party solutions into the CMDB?

options.text: Cloud
Observability
Workflow Automation
Spreadsheet Macros

rationale: Service Graph Connectors are organized into categories such as Cloud (AWS, Azure, GCP) and Observability (monitoring/event sources). These group the certified connectors by the kind of source they ingest. 'Workflow Automation' and 'Spreadsheet Macros' aren't connector categories.

distractor_notes.C: Workflow Automation isn't a Service Graph Connector category.
distractor_notes.D: Spreadsheet Macros is not a connector category at all.

stem: Which TWO ServiceNow solutions automatically create relationships between the CIs/applications that make up an Application Service?

options.text: Discovery
Service Mapping
IntegrationHub ETL
Event Management

rationale: Discovery (horizontal) and Service Mapping (top-down) both build CI relationships automatically as they run — Discovery from infrastructure scanning and Service Mapping from tracing service dependencies. ETL imports/transforms data and Event Management handles alerts; neither auto-builds the application-service relationship graph.

distractor_notes.C: IntegrationHub ETL imports and maps data but doesn't itself discover and create dependency relationships.
distractor_notes.D: Event Management processes events/alerts; it doesn't construct CI relationships.

stem: A CMDB Administrator installs a Service Graph Connector and then customizes its mappings. Which statement describes a consequence?

options.text: The customized mappings are not supported by ServiceNow
Customized fields are automatically tagged as certified in the CMDB
The connector will not run until a change request is attached to each mapping
Customizations are guaranteed to survive every future upgrade untouched

rationale: Once you deviate from the certified, out-of-box mappings, those customizations sit outside ServiceNow's support boundary and you own their upkeep — including reconciling them with future connector updates. That support trade-off is the key thing to weigh before customizing a packaged connector.

distractor_notes.B: Customization doesn't certify fields; if anything it moves them outside the certified set.
distractor_notes.C: No per-mapping change-request gate is imposed on execution.
distractor_notes.D: Customizations are not guaranteed to survive upgrades; related updates may be skipped.

stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe IntegrationHub ETL?

options.text: It integrates third-party data into the CMDB
It uses the IRE to process and integrate data into the CMDB
It performs network discovery to collect infrastructure data
It is only able to import Microsoft SCCM data

rationale: IntegrationHub ETL is a guided transform-and-load tool: it brings third-party data into CMDB (or non-CMDB) tables and, for CMDB targets, processes it through IRE so identification and reconciliation apply. It does not perform discovery, and it's not limited to a single source like SCCM.

distractor_notes.C: Discovery collects infrastructure data; ETL transforms and loads supplied data — it doesn't probe the network.
distractor_notes.D: ETL works with many sources, not just SCCM.

stem: Why would a CMDB Manager use CMDB 360 / Multisource CMDB?

options.text: To identify and compare CI attribute values contributed by multiple data sources
To ingest data from multiple sources using import sets
To perform network discovery of new devices
To approve change requests for CIs

rationale: CMDB 360 / Multisource CMDB is an analysis and visibility tool: it shows, per attribute, what each source reported and how values were reconciled, so managers can spot conflicts and gaps across sources. It isn't itself an ingestion mechanism or a discovery tool.

distractor_notes.B: Import sets are an ingestion method; Multisource CMDB analyzes the resulting multi-source data.
distractor_notes.C: Discovery probes the network; Multisource CMDB inspects already-ingested data.
distractor_notes.D: Change approval is unrelated to multisource visibility.

stem: A Configuration Manager explores CMDB 360 / Multisource saved queries. Which TWO insights can these queries provide?

options.text: Gaps in attribute data across different data sources
Different attribute values reported by different data sources
The physical temperature of servers
The corporate travel budget

rationale: Multisource analysis is about reconciling what each source says: it surfaces where sources disagree on an attribute's value and where a source leaves attributes empty (gaps). Those two insights drive both reconciliation tuning and source-coverage decisions. Temperatures and budgets are unrelated.

distractor_notes.C: Hardware temperature is an operational metric, not a multisource data insight.
distractor_notes.D: Travel budgets have nothing to do with CMDB data.

stem: In ServiceNow Horizontal Discovery, which sequence of phases is correct?

options.text: Scan (port scan) → Classify → Identify → Explore
Explore → Identify → Classify → Scan
Certify → Reconcile → Archive → Destroy
Map → Tag → Approve → Close

rationale: Horizontal Discovery proceeds: a port scan (Shazzam) finds open ports, Classify determines the device type, Identify matches/creates the CI via IRE, and Explore gathers detailed attributes and relationships. The order matters because each phase sets up the next.

distractor_notes.B: That's the phases reversed; you can't explore a device before scanning and classifying it.
distractor_notes.C: Those are lifecycle/governance actions, not Discovery phases.
distractor_notes.D: Map/Tag/Approve/Close aren't the horizontal Discovery phases.

stem: Cloud resources (AWS, Azure, Kubernetes) are labeled with tags like App:Webstore and Env:Prod. Which mapping approach uses these tags to automatically build application services?

options.text: Tag-based service mapping
Top-down pattern-based Service Mapping from a URL entry point
Manual CI creation
Import set coalescing

rationale: Tag-based mapping ingests cloud resource tags to assemble services automatically — fast and well-suited to dynamic cloud estates, though it depends entirely on disciplined tagging. Top-down mapping is more precise but pattern-driven from an entry point; it isn't the tag-driven method described.

distractor_notes.B: Top-down mapping traces dependencies from an entry point via patterns, not from resource tags.
distractor_notes.C: Manual creation is the opposite of automatic tag-based building.
distractor_notes.D: Import set coalescing is a load mechanism, not a service-mapping approach.

stem: After installing the Service Graph Connector Central plugin, where does a Platform Owner get consolidated insight into the different data sources that make up the CMDB?

options.text: The CMDB Workspace
The incident workspace
The knowledge base
The survey designer

rationale: Service Graph Connector Central surfaces source insight within the CMDB Workspace, where configuration managers already monitor health and governance. Centralizing source visibility there keeps data-quality and source management in one role-based place.

distractor_notes.B: The incident workspace is for ITSM incidents, not CMDB source insight.
distractor_notes.C: The knowledge base holds articles, not connector source data.
distractor_notes.D: The survey designer builds surveys, not source dashboards.

references.title: Service Graph Connector Central in CMDB Workspace

stem: A CMDB Administrator must ingest data from Microsoft SCCM with the fastest time to value. Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Service Graph Connectors
Agent Client Collector with custom data collection
Hand-built import sets
Manual CI entry

rationale: For an enterprise source like SCCM, the certified Service Graph Connector delivers value fastest because the integration, mappings, and IRE handling are pre-built. Agent Client Collector requires deploying and configuring agents, and hand-built imports or manual entry are slower and more error-prone.

distractor_notes.B: Agent Client Collector needs agent deployment and configuration — more setup than a packaged connector.
distractor_notes.C: Hand-built import sets require significant mapping/transform work.
distractor_notes.D: Manual entry doesn't scale and is the slowest, least reliable option.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes ServiceNow Discovery from IntegrationHub ETL?

options.text: Discovery actively probes infrastructure to collect data
Both perform active network discovery identically
ETL probes the network and Discovery only loads files
Neither writes to the CMDB

rationale: Discovery goes out and interrogates devices to gather CI data; IntegrationHub ETL takes data from a source and maps/loads it (through IRE for CMDB targets). One collects by probing, the other transforms what's handed to it — different jobs that complement each other.

distractor_notes.B: Only Discovery actively probes; ETL does not.
distractor_notes.C: Reversed — Discovery probes, ETL transforms/loads.
distractor_notes.D: Both can result in CMDB writes; the claim is false.

stem: Does CMDB 360 / Multisource CMDB require ServiceNow Discovery in order to be used?

options.text: No — CI data can come from many sources (integrations, imports, Service Graph Connectors), and reconciliation rules can use any discovery source
Yes — it only works when ITOM Discovery is licensed and running
Yes — it requires all data to come from a single source
No — but it disables all other data sources

rationale: Multisource CMDB is source-agnostic: it analyzes and reconciles data from whatever sources feed the CMDB — Discovery, connectors, imports, integrations — and its reconciliation rules can reference any discovery source. It's not gated on owning ITOM Discovery.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery is one possible source, not a prerequisite for Multisource CMDB.
distractor_notes.C: The whole point is handling multiple sources, not a single one.
distractor_notes.D: It doesn't disable other sources; it embraces them.

stem: A Windows administration team wants to group CIs using CMDB Groups. Which TWO methods can be used to define the group membership?

options.text: Saved queries
Scripted queries
Email rules
Survey responses

rationale: CMDB Group membership can be defined with saved queries (filter-based) or scripted queries (logic-based) so the group dynamically reflects the CIs that match. Email rules and survey responses aren't mechanisms for defining CI group membership.

distractor_notes.C: Email rules route messages; they don't define CI group membership.
distractor_notes.D: Survey responses are unrelated to CMDB group definition.

stem: Compared with the classic Service Mapping map, which TWO are additional capabilities of the Unified Map?

options.text: The number of levels displayed on the map can be modified
Map nodes can be filtered based on user preferences
The map can be zoomed in and out
The map can send approval emails

rationale: Unified Map adds control over how much of the dependency graph you see: you can set how many levels render and filter nodes to the user's preferences, cutting noise on large maps. Zooming is a basic capability common to both maps, and sending approvals isn't a map function.

distractor_notes.C: Zoom is available in both maps, so it isn't an additional capability.
distractor_notes.D: Maps visualize dependencies; they don't send approval emails.

stem: Which engine does IntegrationHub ETL use to efficiently transform and load large volumes of import data into target tables?

options.text: The Robust Transform Engine
The email notification engine
The workflow approval engine
The survey engine

rationale: IntegrationHub ETL leverages the Robust Transform Engine to handle large-scale transform-and-load operations efficiently, mapping source records to target tables (and through IRE for CMDB targets). The notification, approval, and survey engines serve unrelated platform functions.

distractor_notes.B: The notification engine sends messages, not data transforms.
distractor_notes.C: The approval engine governs approvals, not ETL loading.
distractor_notes.D: The survey engine builds surveys, not data pipelines.

stem: Multiple discovery sources will feed the same CI classes. Which practice best keeps the data consistent and duplicate-free across those sources?

options.text: Implement identification and reconciliation rules so CIs are matched and classified consistently regardless of source
Let each source define its own CI class even if results are inconsistent
Write a custom script per source to bypass IRE
Allow each source to write directly to cmdb_ci

rationale: Consistency across sources comes from shared identification and reconciliation rules: every source is matched by the same identifiers and arbitrated by the same reconciliation logic, so you get one CI per real item with standardized classification. Per-source classes or IRE bypasses reintroduce duplicates and drift.

distractor_notes.B: Per-source classes guarantee inconsistency and fragmentation.
distractor_notes.C: Bypassing IRE with custom scripts removes the duplicate-prevention guardrail.
distractor_notes.D: Direct writes to the CI table skip identification entirely.

stem: Discovery probes for an entire datacenter time out and return no data, though the MID Server is up. Which is the most likely first thing to check?

options.text: Network reachability/firewall and credentials between the MID Server and the target devices
The CMDB Health dashboard color scheme
The CSDM domain assignments
The incident assignment rules

rationale: If the MID Server is healthy but probes time out across a whole datacenter, the usual culprit is connectivity — blocked ports/firewall or routing — or credentials that prevent authenticated probes. Verifying the MID Server can actually reach and authenticate to the targets is the logical first step.

distractor_notes.B: Dashboard colors don't affect probe connectivity.
distractor_notes.C: CSDM domain assignments don't cause probe timeouts.
distractor_notes.D: Incident assignment rules are unrelated to Discovery connectivity.

stem: Which ingestion option is the recommended, supported way to bring data from a well-known third-party source into the CMDB with built-in IRE and CSDM alignment?

options.text: A certified Service Graph Connector
A direct Table API insert into cmdb_ci
Manually typing the data
A vendor-provided integration that writes straight to CI tables without IRE

rationale: Certified Service Graph Connectors are the recommended path: they're pre-mapped, run through IRE, and are aligned to CSDM, so third-party data lands cleanly with minimal custom work. Direct API inserts, manual entry, or non-IRE vendor writes all skip the identification/reconciliation that keep the CMDB trustworthy.

distractor_notes.B: A direct Table API insert bypasses IRE and risks duplicates and overwrites.
distractor_notes.C: Manual entry doesn't scale and lacks any automated quality control.
distractor_notes.D: Writing straight to CI tables without IRE is exactly what to avoid.

references.title: Recommended ingestion via Service Graph Connectors

stem: An organization has endpoints that cannot be reached by traditional agentless polling and some that sit in security-restricted network zones. Which approach is best suited to collect CI data from them?

options.text: Agent Client Collector (ACC), using a lightweight agent on the endpoint
Top-down Service Mapping from a URL
Manual CI entry only
Disabling the MID Server

rationale: Agent Client Collector puts a lightweight agent on the endpoint, which is ideal when devices can't be reached by agentless probes or live in restricted zones where opening polling access is undesirable. The agent reports data out rather than requiring the platform to reach in.

distractor_notes.B: Service Mapping traces service dependencies; it isn't an endpoint data-collection method for unreachable devices.
distractor_notes.C: Manual entry doesn't scale and isn't an automated collection method.
distractor_notes.D: Disabling the MID Server removes ingestion capability rather than solving reachability.

stem: A team needs to populate hardware CIs with serial-number data that Discovery cannot collect, sourced from an external system file. What is an appropriate automated ingestion approach?

options.text: A scheduled data import (import set/transform, ideally via IRE) that updates the attributes from the external source
Manually typing each serial number once
Running Discovery more frequently even though it cannot see the data
Deleting the CIs that lack serial numbers

rationale: When data exists in an external source but is non-discoverable, a scheduled import is the right pattern: bring the file in on a cadence and update the CIs (through IRE so identification applies). Re-running Discovery can't surface data it fundamentally can't see, and manual entry won't scale.

distractor_notes.B: Manual entry is unsustainable for ongoing accuracy across many CIs.
distractor_notes.C: More frequent Discovery doesn't help with data Discovery can't collect.
distractor_notes.D: Deleting CIs destroys real records instead of enriching them.

stem: In ServiceNow Discovery, what is the purpose of the initial port scan (Shazzam) phase?

options.text: To detect which ports are open on targets so the device type can be classified
To archive retired CIs
To calculate CMDB Health scores
To approve changes for discovered CIs

rationale: The Shazzam port scan probes target IPs to see which ports respond, which tells Discovery what kind of device it's likely dealing with. That open-port signature feeds the Classify phase, which then drives identification and exploration.

distractor_notes.B: Archiving is a Data Manager lifecycle action, not a Discovery phase.
distractor_notes.C: Health scoring is the Insight layer, not part of port scanning.
distractor_notes.D: Change approval is unrelated to Discovery's scan phase.

stem: Where are the credentials that a MID Server uses to authenticate to discovery targets centrally managed?

options.text: In the platform Credentials store
Hard-coded into each Discovery pattern
In the incident table
In the knowledge base

rationale: Credentials are stored centrally in the platform Credentials store and retrieved securely by the MID Server (using affinity/aliases to pick the right one per target). Centralizing them keeps secrets out of patterns and lets you rotate and govern access in one place.

distractor_notes.B: Hard-coding credentials into patterns is insecure and unmanageable.
distractor_notes.C: The incident table stores incidents, not discovery credentials.
distractor_notes.D: The knowledge base holds articles, not credentials.

stem: What does the Classify phase of Horizontal Discovery determine?

options.text: The type of device/CI (e.g., Windows vs Linux server) so the correct identification and exploration logic is applied
The business owner of the CI
The CMDB Health score
The retirement date of the CI

rationale: Classify uses the scan results to decide what kind of device a target is, which selects the right identifier and pattern for the Identify and Explore phases. Getting classification right is what lets Discovery apply class-appropriate logic rather than a generic guess.

distractor_notes.B: Business ownership is a governance attribute, not what Classify determines.
distractor_notes.C: Health scoring is separate from the Discovery classify step.
distractor_notes.D: Retirement dates are lifecycle data, not a classification output.

stem: An organization wants to ingest AWS and Azure cloud resources into the CMDB. Which is the most appropriate, supported approach?

options.text: Use the certified Cloud Service Graph Connectors / Cloud Discovery for those providers
Manually create a CI for every cloud resource
Write each resource directly to cmdb_ci via a one-off script
Ignore cloud resources entirely

rationale: Cloud estates are large and dynamic, so the supported path is the certified Cloud connectors / Cloud Discovery for AWS, Azure, and GCP — pre-built, IRE-based, and kept current. Manual creation or one-off scripts can't keep pace with cloud churn and skip IRE governance.

distractor_notes.B: Manual creation cannot keep up with elastic cloud resources.
distractor_notes.C: Direct scripted writes bypass IRE and break at the next change.
distractor_notes.D: Ignoring cloud leaves a major part of the estate out of the CMDB.

stem: In an import-based integration, what does the Data Source record define?

options.text: How and from where to retrieve the import data
The CMDB Health threshold
The retirement policy for CIs
The incident priority matrix

rationale: A Data Source record specifies the connection and format for retrieving import data — a file, JDBC query, REST/SOAP endpoint, and so on. It feeds the import set staging table, after which a transform map (ideally via IRE) moves the data to the target CMDB tables.

distractor_notes.B: Health thresholds are an Insight setting, not part of a data source.
distractor_notes.C: Retirement policy is a Data Manager concern.
distractor_notes.D: Incident priority is unrelated to import data sources.

stem: An administrator wants to run Discovery against a single IP address quickly to troubleshoot why a server isn't appearing in the CMDB. Which capability is designed for this?

options.text: Quick Discovery (discover a single target on demand)
CMDB Data Manager destroy policy
A data certification campaign
A CMDB Health dashboard export

rationale: Quick Discovery runs an on-demand scan against a single IP, which is exactly the tool for troubleshooting why one target isn't being created or updated — you get immediate, focused results without waiting for the next scheduled run.

distractor_notes.B: A destroy policy removes CIs; it doesn't troubleshoot discovery of one host.
distractor_notes.C: Certification verifies existing data; it doesn't probe a target.
distractor_notes.D: Exporting a health dashboard doesn't run discovery.

stem: During Horizontal Discovery of an application running on a server, what does Discovery typically create in addition to the application and server CIs?

options.text: A relationship (e.g., 'Runs on::Runs') between the application CI and the host server CI
An incident for each application
A knowledge article for the server
A change request for the application

rationale: Discovery doesn't just create CIs — it wires them together, creating relationships like 'Runs on::Runs' between an application and the server hosting it. Those relationships are what later feed dependency views and service maps, which is much of the CMDB's value.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery creates CIs and relationships, not incidents.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't author knowledge articles.
distractor_notes.D: It doesn't open change requests as part of discovery.

stem: From a security standpoint, what is the recommended practice for the account a MID Server uses to discover targets?

options.text: Use least-privilege credentials scoped to what Discovery needs, managed centrally and rotated
Use a domain administrator account shared across all teams
Embed plaintext credentials in each pattern
Disable credentials so probes run anonymously

rationale: Discovery should follow least privilege: credentials scoped to exactly the read access probes require, stored centrally, and rotated. Over-privileged shared admin accounts and embedded plaintext secrets are security risks, and anonymous probing simply can't collect the authenticated detail Discovery needs.

distractor_notes.B: A shared domain admin account is excessive privilege and a security liability.
distractor_notes.C: Plaintext credentials in patterns are insecure and unmanageable.
distractor_notes.D: Most useful discovery requires authentication; anonymous probes collect little.

stem: A team needs to ingest CMDB data from a popular third-party tool using a certified, low-maintenance integration that maps to CMDB classes through IRE. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A Service Graph Connector
A hand-built outbound REST script
A UI policy
A coalesce-only import with no IRE

rationale: Service Graph Connectors are certified, prebuilt integrations that bring third-party data into the CMDB through IRE, minimizing custom mapping and maintenance. They're the recommended path for supported sources.

distractor_notes.B: A hand-built REST script is more effort and maintenance than a certified connector.
distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior; they don't ingest data.
distractor_notes.D: Bypassing IRE risks duplicates and inconsistent identification.

stem: You have arbitrary external data and need a guided, low-code way to map and transform it into the correct CMDB classes while still going through identification. Which tool is designed for this?

options.text: IntegrationHub ETL
A client script
The Service Portal
A watch list

rationale: IntegrationHub ETL provides a guided, robust transform experience to map external data into CMDB classes, feeding the data through IRE for identification and reconciliation. It's built for flexible source-to-CMDB mapping.

distractor_notes.B: Client scripts run on forms, not server-side ETL.
distractor_notes.C: The Service Portal is an end-user interface.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.

stem: An organization wants to populate CIs for on-premises servers and network gear without installing agents on each device. Which approach fits?

options.text: Agentless Discovery via a MID Server
Manual CI entry for every device
A Service Portal widget
A coalesce field

rationale: Discovery is agentless and uses a MID Server to probe infrastructure and populate CIs through IRE — ideal for on-prem servers and network devices without per-device agents.

distractor_notes.B: Manual entry doesn't scale and goes stale quickly.
distractor_notes.C: A portal widget is UI, not infrastructure discovery.
distractor_notes.D: Coalesce matches import records.

stem: A team wants continuous, agent-based collection of configuration and health data directly from endpoints. Which capability is intended for this?

options.text: Agent Client Collector (ACC)
Agentless Discovery only
A transform map
The Service Catalog

rationale: Agent Client Collector uses a lightweight agent on endpoints for continuous data collection, complementing agentless Discovery when you want ongoing, host-resident telemetry.

distractor_notes.B: Agentless Discovery is periodic and host-external — not agent-based continuous collection.
distractor_notes.C: Transform maps move imported data.
distractor_notes.D: The Service Catalog is for ordering services.

stem: Business-context attributes like application owner and business criticality can't be discovered automatically. How are these typically populated?

options.text: Through manual entry or import for non-discoverable data
Only through agentless Discovery
They cannot exist in the CMDB
Via a UI policy

rationale: Some attributes aren't discoverable (ownership, criticality, business context) and are populated by manual entry or import — ideally still passing through IRE for consistency.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery can't infer business context like ownership.
distractor_notes.C: Such attributes absolutely belong in the CMDB; they're just sourced differently.
distractor_notes.D: UI policies change form behavior; they don't source data.

stem: Regardless of whether data arrives via Discovery, a Service Graph Connector, or ETL, the organization wants consistent duplicate prevention. What ensures this consistency?

options.text: All ingestion paths write through IRE
Each path uses its own separate database
A coalesce field on the form
The Service Portal

rationale: Because Discovery, Service Graph Connectors, ETL, import, and API all write through IRE, identification and reconciliation are applied consistently — so duplicate prevention doesn't depend on the path.

distractor_notes.B: There's one CMDB; paths don't use separate databases.
distractor_notes.C: A form coalesce field doesn't govern multi-source ingestion.
distractor_notes.D: The Service Portal is unrelated to ingestion identity.

stem: Discovery needs to reach devices inside the corporate network from the cloud instance without exposing inbound ports. What component makes this possible?

options.text: A MID Server using outbound connections
An inbound firewall rule to each device
A coalesce field
A catalog item

rationale: The MID Server runs inside the network and initiates outbound connections to the instance, executing Discovery probes against internal devices without exposing inbound ports.

distractor_notes.B: Opening inbound ports per device is the exposure the MID Server avoids.
distractor_notes.C: Coalesce matches import records.
distractor_notes.D: Catalog items are orderable services.

stem: A source system already holds authoritative inventory data in its own database, and you want to bring it into the CMDB rather than re-scan the environment. Which approach is more appropriate?

options.text: Ingest the existing data
Run Discovery to rediscover everything from scratch
Manually retype each record
Use a UI policy

rationale: When an authoritative source already has the data, ingesting it (via a Service Graph Connector or IntegrationHub ETL) is more efficient than re-discovering. Discovery shines for scanning the live environment, not re-importing known inventory.

distractor_notes.B: Re-discovering duplicates effort when an authoritative source already exists.
distractor_notes.C: Manual retyping doesn't scale and is error-prone.
distractor_notes.D: UI policies don't ingest data.

stem: Which statement best describes the role of IntegrationHub ETL versus a Service Graph Connector?

options.text: ETL offers flexible custom mapping of arbitrary sources
They are identical with different names
ETL only works for Discovery data
Service Graph Connectors bypass IRE

rationale: IntegrationHub ETL is the flexible, build-your-own mapping tool for arbitrary sources, while Service Graph Connectors are certified, prebuilt integrations for specific products. Both feed the CMDB through IRE.

distractor_notes.B: They serve different purposes — custom mapping vs certified prebuilt.
distractor_notes.C: ETL handles arbitrary external data, not just Discovery output.
distractor_notes.D: Service Graph Connectors use IRE; they don't bypass it.

stem: To keep the CMDB trustworthy as new sources are onboarded, what is a recommended ingestion practice?

options.text: Route all sources through IRE and define reconciliation precedence for overlapping attributes
Give every source equal authority over all attributes
Disable identification rules for speed
Write directly to cmdb_ci, skipping IRE

rationale: Routing sources through IRE and setting reconciliation precedence prevents duplicates and stops weaker sources from overwriting trusted data. Equal authority or bypassing IRE undermines data quality.

distractor_notes.B: Equal authority causes attribute thrashing between sources.
distractor_notes.C: Disabling identification produces duplicates.
distractor_notes.D: Skipping IRE bypasses identification/reconciliation entirely.

stem: Which TWO are valid ways to populate the CMDB?

options.text: Agentless Discovery via a MID Server
A Service Graph Connector for a certified source
A UI policy on the incident form
A watch list

rationale: Discovery and Service Graph Connectors are both legitimate ingestion methods (along with ETL, import, and API), all flowing through IRE. UI policies and watch lists are unrelated to CMDB population.

distractor_notes.C: UI policies change form behavior; they don't populate CIs.
distractor_notes.D: Watch lists handle notifications.

stem: Which TWO statements about ingestion are correct?

options.text: Discovery is well suited to scanning the live environment for CIs
IntegrationHub ETL is well suited to mapping arbitrary external data into CMDB classes
Ingestion paths each maintain their own separate CMDB
Discovery requires an agent on every device

rationale: Discovery scans the live environment; ETL flexibly maps external data into CMDB classes. There's one CMDB shared across paths, and Discovery is agentless.

distractor_notes.C: All paths write to the single CMDB through IRE.
distractor_notes.D: Discovery is agentless via the MID Server.
